title: Lifting Biomolecular Data Acquisition
claim: Measuring one item per experiment mostly yields null signal; testing mixtures per experiment captures sparse signal and yields more informative data.
layout: 2 rows by 3 columns, top baseline vs bottom ours, left-to-right
description: Two rows of three panels contrast one-sequence-per-cell testing with multi-sequence mixtures. The top row (a–c) shows three grey cells, each with one colored antibody over a pink core. Next to them is a sparse activity-versus-sequence plot with one blue spike and a single rectangular bump, then a dataset list D of (x_i, 0.0) pairs in red. The bottom row (d–f) shows cells loaded with several differently colored antibodies. Next to them is the same sparse plot with six blue spikes, one landing inside the bump, then a dataset list D of (mu_i, value) pairs with values 0.1, 0.0 and 0.5 in blue. The eye goes first to the colorful antibodies, then to the spikes and the red zeros versus blue nonzero values.
caption: Lifting data acquisition Top row: learn from (x, y) pairs. a. Test one sequence per cell. b. When the sequence-activity map f is sparse (black), most sequences (blue) show no activity. c. So the resulting dataset contains little information. Bottom row: learn from mixtures µi(x) = Pmi
abstract: One strategy to scale up ML-driven science is to increase wet lab experiments' information density. We present a method based on a neural extension of compressed sensing to function space. We measure the activity of multiple different molecules simultaneously, rather than individually. Then, we deconvolute the molecule-activity map during model training. Co-design of wet lab experiments and learning algorithms provably leads to orders-of-magnitude gains in information density. We demonstrate on antibodies and cell therapies.
